title: Why flying costs more: jet fuel, surcharges and new fare rules
dek: Jet fuel has risen four months in a row, airlines have added fuel surcharges, and the government has given itself new powers over ticket prices from January.
seoTitle: Airfares and jet fuel prices India 2026: timeline
bigLabel: Price of jet fuel (ATF) for domestic airlines in Delhi from 1 November 2026, after a fourth monthly rise in a row

glance.what: Jet fuel, also called aviation turbine fuel or ATF, makes up roughly 35–40% of an airline's costs. Since the Strait of Hormuz closed, its price in India has kept climbing, and airlines have added fuel surcharges to tickets. On 2 November the government notified rules that let it cap fares in an "extraordinary situation".
glance.why: Higher fuel costs mean higher fares and fewer flights. Airlines scheduled 2.6% fewer weekly flights in November than in October 2025, and domestic passenger numbers fell 6.5% year on year in September.
glance.next: The Supreme Court hears a petition on high fares on 16 November. Jet fuel prices are revised on the 1st of each month, and the new fare rules take effect on 1 January 2027.

forYou: Fuel surcharges are part of the ticket price, so compare the total fare, not the base fare. From 1 January 2027, airlines must show a full breakup: base fare, taxes, fees, cancellation charges and refund conditions. Booking early and avoiding festival dates is still the main way to pay less.

events.title: Airlines get to set their own fares
events.summary: Background: India stops fixing airfares and lets airlines price tickets according to the market. Until now, the regulator could step in only over excessive or predatory pricing.

events.title: Jet fuel doubles for foreign airlines; domestic rise capped
events.summary: With the Strait of Hormuz closed, jet fuel for foreign airlines and charter operators in Delhi more than doubles to ₹2,07,341 per kilolitre. Domestic airlines get a smaller, staggered rise of 8.56% to ₹1,04,927 per kilolitre (about ₹104.93 a litre), which the oil ministry says is to protect domestic travel costs.

events.title: Jet fuel up ₹5 a litre
events.summary: Oil companies raise the price of jet fuel for domestic airlines by ₹5 a litre, the first of four monthly increases in a row.

events.title: Up ₹6.28 a litre
events.summary: Jet fuel in Delhi rises by ₹6.28 to ₹121.28 a litre.

events.title: The biggest monthly jump: up about ₹16
events.summary: Jet fuel rises 13.22%, or nearly ₹16 a litre, to ₹137.12 in Delhi.

events.title: Airlines add fuel surcharges
events.summary: IndiGo raises its fuel charges first. Akasa Air, Air India and Air India Express follow with surcharges on new bookings from 9 October: ₹375 to ₹1,150 on Akasa's domestic flights and ₹400 to ₹1,200 on Air India's, depending on distance, and up to $215 each way on Air India's North America flights. The airlines call the surcharges temporary.
events.differs: Business Today dates IndiGo's increase to 5 October; InsideFlyer says 6 October.

events.title: Fourth monthly rise in a row
events.summary: Jet fuel in Delhi rises to ₹138.50 a litre. According to IATA's fuel price monitor, India's domestic jet fuel costs roughly 28% more than the global average.
events.differs: Reports give the increase as ₹1.30, ₹1.37 or ₹1.38 a litre.

events.title: Supreme Court: "Don't travel by air"
events.summary: The Supreme Court refuses to urgently hear a request in a public-interest case against high fares. "Don't travel by air. Next case," says Justice Vikram Nath. The main case, which asks for limits on surge pricing and festival-season fare caps, continues, with a hearing on 16 November.

events.title: New rules let the government cap fares
events.summary: The civil aviation ministry notifies Rule 192 of the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026. The government can order limits on fares in an "extraordinary situation", for a set period. Airlines must publish fares and show a full breakup of base fare, taxes, fees and cancellation charges, and the DGCA will monitor fares. The rules apply from 1 January 2027. Some experts quoted by the Free Press Journal say the rules do not define an extraordinary situation.
